html:
SMTO-SYS-0002 — SMTO hit an internal problem and stopped this task

GUID: d3f35993-10d7-4ca1-a5dc-61abef4e5eb8
Slug: internal-runtime-fault
Domain: SYS · Subsystem: runtime

What happened

  • Something went wrong inside SMTO itself, not in the command or service it was using, so it stopped this task. This message does not tell us what caused the problem, and a step already in progress may have finished.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether your action already happened. Look at the last step in the task's activity, then check the result itself, such as the file, message or change. SMTO may have started that step before the problem, so repeating it could do it twice.
  2. Type /restart to restart SMTO, then open the task and select Resume, or Restart task if Resume isn't shown. The restart also interrupts other running tasks. The task stays blocked until SMTO restarts, because the problem is in the copy of SMTO that was running.
  3. If it stops again with this message, select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. This message does not establish what completed or why it failed; the error details point to the exact place in SMTO.

What success looks like

  • After the restart, the task continues past the step where it stopped.

If it still fails

  • There is no confirmed quick fix for this message alone. Send the copied error details to the person who manages SMTO, and don't change settings or delete data to guess at a fix.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • SMTO's runtime raised an internal fault (import failure, missing API, signature mismatch, invariant or lost control contract) rather than a target command error; the run is blocked for this server instance and earlier execution records are kept.

What this means

  • Runtime fault classification establishes an owned internal import/API/signature/invariant failure, or an explicit internal-fault boundary reports loss of its required execution/control contract. Internal fault classification cannot replace operation effect evidence. A capability may already have dispatched before its adapter faults; neither a runtime defect nor a legacy text label proves that prior work never ran.

Why this can happen

  • Runtime fault classification establishes an owned internal import/API/signature/invariant failure, or an explicit internal-fault boundary reports loss of its required execution/control contract.

How to diagnose it

  • Preserve occurrence ID, fault fingerprint, server generation and boundary; inspect remote_effect_possible and original receipts separately.

How to fix it

  • No direct repair is available for this occurrence. Use the supported investigation or alternative workflow below.
  • Find the runtime.fault_blocked event (fingerprint, module, function, code) for the run and the matching traceback in the runtime fault audit; the blocker is scoped to the current server_generation_id. Reconcile any unknown_operations against external state, fix or report the defect, then restart the Server so the blocker resolves before resuming. Do not delete evidence or invent a configuration change.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The internal defect is repaired and existing effect uncertainty is reconciled before resuming work.

What not to do

  • Do not delete evidence or invent a configuration change for an unexplained internal failure.

Technical notes

  • Internal fault classification cannot replace operation effect evidence. A capability may already have dispatched before its adapter faults; neither a runtime defect nor a legacy text label proves that prior work never ran.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
